title: The hypertrophy series: baseline within session vs baseline between sessions
summary: NH separates baseline within a session (recovering between sets) from baseline between sessions (full recovery for the next workout). Both stabilize tonnage, signal when to progress, tell you when to end a session, and validate a program, which should be tested for 2-4 weeks like a software beta.
claims: Baseline acts both as a recovery tool between sessions and as a way to regulate intensity between sets within a session
Baseline matters because controlling how long you need to repeat an effort stabilises tonnage so it never dips
Volume/intensity calculations are worthless without gym experience; treat a new program like software with an alpha test on paper and a beta test in the gym
Test a new program for 2-4 weeks, running at least two or three cycles; that is enough to expose what does not work
Getting the same reps on every set (e.g. 4 reps on all four sets) means the weight is not challenging enough
Dropping from 8 reps on the first set to 5 is too steep a loss and signals a programming or weight-selection problem
Exercise order changes recovery: a lift done third behaves differently when done first, which is why rotating exercises too much muddles programming
When a muscle can no longer stay above your intensity threshold, it is done for the day; stop its work there to keep the session tight and quick
If you can't repeat a knee flexion effort three days later, you weren't recovered for strength work; swap in a lighter variation in a different rep range
Some lifters want full recovery before hitting a muscle again, others partial or over-recovery; all are valid if justified by volume, intensity and tonnage
He can do heavy hip hinges frequently, but heavy knee flexion wrecks his recovery
Baseline is the positive counterpart of injury: both tell you something went wrong, but baseline is muscular, kinder, and gives feedback every session
Hypertrophy is tiring the muscle as much as possible without injury, letting it recover enough to progress, then working it again as soon as you can
Even for a muscle you want to shrink, baseline principles govern how hard to push it
